why: AI engineer has become one of the most sought-after profiles, in Tunisia and abroad, especially for remote work with European companies. Before you build applications, you need to understand what the job is and how an LLM works inside: tokens, cost, limits.
outcome: explain what an AI engineer does, understand tokens, the context window and hallucinations, compute the cost of a request with the real prices, choose a model, and make your first call to Claude in Python, safely.

lessons.title: What does an AI engineer do?
text: An AI engineer is a developer who builds applications with artificial intelligence inside: a chatbot that answers customers, a tool that reads invoices and pulls data out of them, an assistant that helps a support team... They don't train the model from scratch: they use ready-made models such as Claude through an API, and they think about the whole product: the prompt, the data sent, the code around the model, the cost, security, and how the thing works well in production and improves over time.

People often mix up these jobs. A data scientist analyses data and builds statistical models to answer business questions. An ML engineer trains and deploys machine learning models (sometimes from scratch) and works a lot with data pipelines and GPUs. A software developer builds regular applications. The AI engineer sits in the middle: they have a developer's reflexes (clean code, tests, APIs, deployment) and add an understanding of LLMs on top: prompts, evaluation, cost and limits.

The skills in demand: solid Python (a bit of JavaScript helps), REST APIs and JSON, Git, some SQL, and an understanding of LLMs. Later you add tool use and agents, RAG and vector databases, evaluation, monitoring. Soft skills matter too: explaining to a client what AI can and cannot do, and writing clearly, because a prompt is writing too.

The market: in Tunisia, startups and IT services firms (ESN) work on AI projects for European clients, and some European companies hire Tunisian juniors remotely. Freelancing works too (chatbots, automation, integrations), but you need a portfolio that stands out. This track goes step by step: the basics now, then prompt engineering, then the Claude API in detail, tool use and agents, RAG, and finally production: monitoring, cost and evaluation.
points: AI engineer = a developer who builds products with ready-made models, not a researcher who trains models.
An ML engineer trains and deploys models; a data scientist analyses data; an AI engineer integrates LLMs into a product.
Python, APIs, JSON and Git are the foundation; understanding LLMs comes on top.
A portfolio of real projects helps you more than a long list of certificates.

lessons.title: How an LLM works: tokens and the next token
text: An LLM (Large Language Model) is a model trained on a huge amount of text. The core idea is simple: you give it the beginning of a text, and it predicts the next piece. It doesn't understand like a human: it computes probabilities, gives a score to every possible piece, and picks one. Then it appends that piece to the text and repeats, piece by piece, until the answer is complete.

That piece is called a token. A token is not always a word: it can be a whole word, half a word, a few characters, or punctuation. The model doesn't read characters directly: the text is split into tokens, and each token has a number. Most of the time, text in a language other than English, such as Derja or Arabic, takes more tokens for the same meaning, and that affects the cost and the room left in the prompt.

There are two stages. Training: the company that builds the model runs huge amounts of text through it and adjusts billions of parameters until it predicts the next token well, then adds a stage so it follows instructions and is helpful and safe. This is very expensive and you don't do it. Inference: when you send a prompt through the API and the model produces an answer. The model does not learn from your conversation: its parameters don't change.

This is why the model can be wrong. It picks the text that looks plausible given what it learned, not what has been checked. If the information wasn't in the training data, is outdated, or the question is vague, it gives you a tidy, confident answer... that is wrong. On top of that, the model has a date limit on its knowledge (the knowledge cutoff), and it doesn't know what happened after it unless you give it in the prompt.
points: An LLM predicts the next token, token by token, until the answer is complete.
Token = a piece of text; cost and limits are all counted in tokens, not words.
Training is done once by the provider; inference is what you run with every request.
A tidy, confident answer is not necessarily a correct one.

example.code:
Prompt: "The capital of Tunisia is"

Scores for the next token (illustration, not real numbers):
  " Tunis"   0.92
  " a"       0.03
  " the"     0.02
  ...

Chosen: " Tunis" -> appended to the text,
then the model predicts the next token again.
example.note: The model doesn't 'know' the answer: it picks the most likely token given what it learned.

lessons.title: Context window, tokens and cost
text: The context window is the largest number of tokens the model can see in one request: the system prompt, the conversation history, the documents you included, and the answer it will write. In Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, the context window is 1M (one million) tokens, and output goes up to 128K tokens. But 'can' doesn't mean 'should': you pay for every token you send.

The API has no memory: every request must send the whole conversation from the start. So in a chatbot, every new message makes the input bigger, and the cost grows with it. Billing uses two numbers: input tokens (what you send) and output tokens (what the model produces), and output always costs more. Prices in dollars per million tokens (input / output): Opus 5.5 $4 / $20, Sonnet 5.5 $2 / $10, Haiku 5.5 $0.10 / $0.50 (if the prompt stays under 100K tokens; above that $0.50 / $2.50), and Fable 5.1, the most capable, $10 / $50.

The calculation is simple: cost = input_tokens × input_price / 1,000,000 + output_tokens × output_price / 1,000,000. Example: a request with 2,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens on Opus 5.5: 2,000 × 4 / 1M = $0.008, and 500 × 20 / 1M = $0.010, total $0.018. Looks like nothing? But with 10,000 requests a day, that's $180 a day. The same work on Haiku 5.5 comes to $4.50 a day. That's why the choice of model and the length of the prompt matter so much.

To know the exact numbers, don't guess: the response contains response.usage.input_tokens and response.usage.output_tokens, and before sending you can use client.messages.count_tokens. Don't use tiktoken: it's OpenAI's tokenizer and gives wrong counts for Claude. Also know that the model's thinking (its reasoning before the answer) is part of the output and counts toward max_tokens, and you can control it with output_config effort. In the next courses we'll look at prompt caching and the Batches API (50% cheaper) to bring the bill down.
points: Context window = input + output in one request; 1M tokens on the new models.
The API is stateless: every request sends the whole history again.
With Claude, an output token costs 5 times more than an input token.
Measure with usage and count_tokens, don't guess, and don't use tiktoken.

example.note: Result: Opus 5.5 180.00, Sonnet 5.5 90.00, Haiku 5.5 4.50 dollars a day.

lessons.title: Model families: how to choose a model
text: Anthropic offers Claude at several levels. Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) is the default model: very strong at code, reasoning and long tasks. Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) gives good quality at half the price. Haiku 5.5 (claude-haiku-5-5) is the fastest and cheapest, great for high volume: classification, extraction, routing. And Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1) is the most capable, for the hardest tasks, but more expensive. Use these ids exactly as they are, with no date at the end.

There are other providers: OpenAI (GPT), Google (Gemini), Mistral (a French company), and 'open weights' models such as Llama or Mistral that you can run on your own machine or server, for example with Ollama. Open models are useful when data must not leave your premises or when you want to control everything, but you need GPUs and hosting work, and most of the time the quality is below the big models.

The choice is always a trade-off between 5 things: quality (does it understand and reason well?), speed (latency, important for a chatbot), cost (the token price and how many tokens it uses), privacy (where the data goes and who can see it), and hosting (cloud API or your own server). There is no 'best model' in absolute terms: there is a best model for a given task on a given budget.

A practical method: start with a strong model (Opus 5.5) to see the quality ceiling. Then build a small test set of real examples (20 or 50 cases) and try Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 on them. If the cheaper model gets the same result on your case, take the cheaper one. You can also mix: Haiku classifies the tickets and Opus answers the hard ones. Remember that the real cost is the cost of the whole task: a cheap model that gets it wrong and makes you retry 3 times can end up more expensive.
points: Opus 5.5 = the default; Sonnet 5.5 = the middle; Haiku 5.5 = cheap and fast; Fable 5.1 = the most capable.
Open models = control and privacy, but GPUs and maintenance.
Test on your own examples, not on internet leaderboards.
Measure the cost of the whole task, not just the token price.

example.note: A small router: each task gets the model that is good enough for it, and the choice is decided by tests.

lessons.title: Hallucinations: why the model gets it wrong and how to reduce it
text: A hallucination is when the model gives you wrong information with full confidence: a reference that doesn't exist, a function that isn't in a library, made-up numbers, an incorrect law. The cause is how it works: it predicts plausible text, it doesn't look anything up in a database. When information is missing, the model usually fills the gap with something that sounds right instead of saying 'I don't know'.

The most common cases: questions about small, little-known things (a small Tunisian company, a new law), exact numbers and dates, sources and references, and information that came after the knowledge cutoff. Add vague prompts: if you don't tell it what to use and what not to, it fills in on its own.

How to reduce it: first, grounding: put the right documents in the prompt and tell it to answer only from those documents. That's the idea behind RAG, which we'll see later. Second: give it permission to say 'I don't know' and tell it exactly what to say. Third: ask it to quote the sentence from the document it relied on, so you can check. Fourth: whenever you can, check with code: is the JSON valid? does the function exist? is the calculation right?

The golden rule: don't trust the answer blindly, especially when money, health, law or decisions about people are involved. A good AI engineer builds a system with verification: tests, evaluation on examples, and a human reviewing when the risk is high. And tell users the truth: AI can be wrong.
points: Hallucination = a confident wrong answer; normal for an LLM, not a rare bug.
Grounding: give it the source and tell it to answer only from it.
Permission to say 'I don't know' + quoting the source = easier verification.
Check with code and with a human, depending on the risk.

example.code:
System:
You answer questions about our company's leave policy.
Use ONLY the document between <policy> tags.
If the answer is not in the document, say exactly:
"I don't know, please ask HR."
Quote the sentence of the document you used.

<policy>
...the current HR policy text...
</policy>

User:
How many days of annual leave do I get after 3 years?
example.note: Grounding + permission to say 'I don't know' + quoting: three techniques in one prompt.

lessons.title: Your first call to Claude in Python
text: Installation: pip install anthropic (preferably in a virtual environment). Then you need an API key from the Anthropic Console. To pay, the account asks for an international payment card; in Tunisia, many people use an international technology card (carte technologique internationale) or a company card. This key is a secret, like a password: whoever gets it can use your account at your expense.

Why an environment variable? Because code goes to Git, to colleagues, to GitHub, and a key written in the code gets stolen fast. The SDK reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment on its own. On Linux or macOS: export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... ; in PowerShell: $env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = "..." ; or a .env file that you add to .gitignore.

The call: client = anthropic.Anthropic(), then client.messages.create with model, max_tokens (the maximum length of the output) and messages: a list of {role, content} dictionaries, where the first is always 'user'. You can add system to set the role and the rules. The API has no memory: to hold a conversation, you add the answer with the 'assistant' role and send everything again. Don't set temperature or a prefill copied from old tutorials: the new models reject them with a 400 error. To control depth and cost, there is output_config={"effort": ...} (on Opus 5.5 the default is medium).

The response: response.content is a list of blocks (text, thinking, tool_use...), so check block.type before reading .text. response.usage contains input_tokens and output_tokens. And above all, check response.stop_reason: 'end_turn' finished normally, 'max_tokens' the answer was cut (raise max_tokens), 'tool_use' it wants to use a tool, 'refusal' it refused. The SDK retries on its own on 429 and 5xx, and you can catch errors such as anthropic.AuthenticationError or anthropic.RateLimitError.
points: pip install anthropic, and the key in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, never in the code.
messages.create = model + max_tokens + messages (+ system).
Check stop_reason before reading the content, and block.type before .text.
usage tells you what you paid: log it from day one.

example.note: A complete call: system, message, stop_reason check, reading the text and the usage.

lessons.title: Data, privacy and responsibility
text: Everything you send to an API leaves your premises and goes to the provider's servers. Before sending, ask yourself: does the model need to see this data? Personal data (names, phone numbers, addresses, national ID (CIN) numbers, health or banking data), secrets (API keys, passwords), and the company's confidential code or documents: none of it gets sent without a need and permission.

Companies have rules: some allow no AI tool at all, some allow one provider under contract, some require an open model on their own servers. In Europe there is the GDPR, and in Tunisia there is the personal data protection law and the INPDP. As a junior, never put client data into an AI tool 'just to try': ask first, always.

A practical method: minimise the data (send only what's needed), hide personal data behind placeholders such as [EMAIL] and [PHONE] before the call, don't keep users' full texts in logs without a reason, and know what the provider does with the data (retention, contract). Masking with regex is a good start but not complete: names, for example, are hard to catch with a regex.

Responsibility too: models can reproduce biases from their training data (gender, origin, language...). Don't let a model make a decision about people on its own (hiring, credit) without human control. And be clear with users: tell them they are talking to an AI, not a human, and that the answer can be wrong. That transparency builds trust, and in many places it has become a legal obligation.
points: Send the minimum; hide personal data before the API.
Ask about the company's rules before using any AI tool.
Bias is real: sensitive decisions need a human.
Tell users they are talking to an AI.

example.code:
import re

def mask_personal_data(text: str) -> str:
    # Replace e-mails and Tunisian phone numbers before sending text to an external API
    text = re.sub(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+", "[EMAIL]", text)
    text = re.sub(r"(\+216\s?)?\b\d{2}\s?\d{3}\s?\d{3}\b", "[PHONE]", text)
    return text

ticket = "Client Sami, sami.benali@example.com, tel +216 22 123 456, cannot log in."
print(mask_personal_data(ticket))
# Client Sami, [EMAIL], tel [PHONE], cannot log in.
example.note: The name 'Sami' is still there: regex is a start, not complete protection.

lessons.title: How to learn and keep improving: projects and portfolio
text: AI changes fast: new models, new features, and tutorials go stale within months. So the biggest skill is learning on your own. Read the provider's official documentation before articles and videos, because it's the one that changes with the API. When you find a tutorial using a parameter that no longer works (such as temperature on the new Claude), you'll know why.

Practice: small, finished projects beat a big project that never ends. Examples: a support ticket classifier (Derja, French, Arabic), a tool that extracts information from PDF invoices into JSON, a chatbot that answers from a product's documentation, a script that compares the cost of 3 models on the same task. Each project shows a skill: prompting, API, evaluation, cost.

Portfolio: every project on GitHub with a clear README: the problem, how it works, the results (how many correct out of how many examples, how much it costs), the limits, and how to run it. Never put the API key in the repo: .env in .gitignore. A recruiter in Europe prefers one small project measured with numbers over 10 chatbot projects without a single test.

Organisation: 5 to 7 hours a week on this track will move you forward well. For each course: read the lessons, do the exercises yourself, and add something small of your own. Internet down? Prepare the code and prompts offline and try the calls when it's back. And to avoid spending too much while learning: Haiku 5.5 for experiments, a small max_tokens, and keep an eye on usage. Don't forget the community: Tunisian tech meetups and groups can help you find a mentor, feedback on your projects, and opportunities.
points: Official documentation before any tutorial.
Small finished projects, each showing a clear skill.
A README with measured results and limits = a portfolio that stands out.
Experiment with Haiku 5.5 and a small max_tokens to keep the cost down.

exercises.q: A request has 3,000 input tokens and 800 output tokens on claude-sonnet-5-5. How much does it cost? And how much with 5,000 requests a day?
exercises.hint: Sonnet 5.5: $2 input and $10 output per million tokens.

exercises.q: Write a function read_answer(response) that returns the text of the answer, returns None on a refusal, and prints a warning when the answer was cut.
exercises.hint: Check stop_reason, and join only the blocks whose type is 'text'.

exercises.q: Explain in 3 sentences the difference between an AI engineer and an ML engineer, as you would in an interview.
exercises.answer: An ML engineer trains models (sometimes from scratch) and deploys them, working on data, features and GPUs. An AI engineer uses ready-made models such as Claude through an API and builds a product with them: prompts, integration, evaluation, cost and production. Both are developers, but the AI engineer focuses more on the product and on the LLM's behaviour, not on training.

exercises.q: Choose a model for each case and justify: (a) classifying 200,000 emails a day, (b) an assistant that reviews long contracts, (c) a regular support chatbot.
exercises.hint: Think about volume, difficulty and cost.
exercises.answer: (a) claude-haiku-5-5: high volume and a simple task, cost and speed matter most. (b) claude-opus-5-5: long documents and hard reasoning; claude-fable-5-1 if the quality isn't enough. (c) claude-sonnet-5-5 to start, then try Haiku 5.5 on your own examples. In every case, decide with tests on your own data, not on gut feeling.

System:
You answer questions about our products using ONLY the price list below.
If the answer is not in the price list, say exactly: "I don't have this information."

</price_list>

exercises.q: Write code that counts the tokens of a file report.txt before sending it, and estimates the input cost on Opus 5.5.
exercises.hint: client.messages.count_tokens with the same model, and $4 per million input tokens.
exercises.answer:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

with open("report.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    text = f.read()

count = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}],
)
input_cost = count.input_tokens * 4 / 1_000_000  # Opus 5.5: 4 USD per million input tokens
print(count.input_tokens, "tokens, about", round(input_cost, 4), "USD of input")

exercises.q: A support ticket contains: the customer's name, email, phone number, bank card number, and a description of the problem. What do you send to the API to classify it?
exercises.answer: Only the description of the problem, after hiding any personal data in it (email, phone, name) behind placeholders. The bank card number is never sent. The name, email and phone aren't needed for classification: keep them on your side and link them to the result through the ticket id.

pitfalls: Writing the API key in the code or pushing it to GitHub: the key gets stolen and the bill is yours. Always an environment variable, and .env in .gitignore.
Reading response.content[0].text directly: the first block isn't always text, and if stop_reason is 'refusal' or 'max_tokens' the answer is incomplete.
Trusting the answer blindly: numbers, references and functions need checking, especially for sensitive matters.
Sending a whole document or a long history with every request without measuring: the cost climbs fast. Watch usage from day one.
Sending personal data or confidential code to an API without a need and without the company's permission.
Copying code from an old tutorial (temperature, prefill, a dated model id): the new models reject it with a 400 error.
Counting Claude tokens with tiktoken: the count is wrong; use usage or count_tokens.

interview.q: What is the difference between an AI engineer and an ML engineer?
interview.a: An ML engineer trains and deploys models, and works on data and training. An AI engineer builds products with ready-made models through an API: prompts, integration into the application, evaluation, cost and monitoring. At junior level, an AI engineer needs a software engineer's reflexes more than the maths of training.

interview.q: What is a token and why does it matter?
interview.a: A token is a piece of text (a word, part of a word, punctuation) that the model reads and writes with. The context window, max_tokens and billing are all in tokens, so the length of the prompt and the answer directly affects cost and latency. Text in a language other than English usually takes more tokens.

interview.q: Why does an LLM hallucinate, and how do you reduce the risk?
interview.a: Because it predicts the text closest to what it learned; it doesn't check a source. I reduce it with grounding (I put the documents in the prompt and tell it to answer only from them), I give it permission to say 'I don't know', I ask it to quote the source, and I check with code or a human depending on the risk. And I run an evaluation on examples before production.

interview.q: How do you estimate the monthly cost of a chatbot?
interview.a: I measure the average input and output tokens per request (with usage on a prototype, or count_tokens), multiply them by the model's price (for example Opus 5.5 at $4 / $20 per million), and multiply by the number of requests per month. I don't forget that the history grows with every message. Then I look at the levers: a cheaper model for some tasks, a shorter prompt, caching, batch.

interview.q: How do you choose between a large model and a small one?
interview.a: I start with a strong model to know the quality ceiling, build a test set from real cases, and try the cheaper models on it. I take the cheapest one that reaches the required level. I count the cost of the whole task: a cheap model that gets it wrong and retries can end up more expensive.

interview.q: What is the context window, and what happens when the conversation gets very long?
interview.a: It's the maximum number of tokens in one request: system, history, documents and output. As the conversation grows, cost and latency grow, and if we go over the limit the request is rejected. We handle it: we trim or summarise the old history, and send only the documents that are needed.

interview.q: How do you protect the API key and users' data?
interview.a: The key goes in an environment variable or a secret manager, never in the code or the repo, with one key per environment. For data: I send the minimum, hide personal data before the call, don't log full texts without a reason, and follow the company's rules and laws such as the GDPR.

interview.q: Does the Claude API remember the conversation? How do you build a chatbot with many messages?
interview.a: No, the Messages API is stateless. The application keeps the history and sends all of it with every request: messages with the 'user' and 'assistant' roles, in order. That means the input grows with every turn, and you have to account for it in the cost.
